To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the subsidiaries' change management processes are shaped by global and national institutional effects.
globalization and national diversities are not mutually exclusive, but rather intertwined, and that the effects of both are contingent.
(a) global convergence is shaped by national diversities; and (b) national diversities are shaped by global convergence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between the global and the national.
the `how' of globalizing MNCs and the `why' of the national differences.
the interplay of global convergence and national diversities in MNCs' subsidiaries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the globalization of MNCs does not mean the homogenization of their work systems.
there is no single best way to globalize in MNCs, and that the global and local effects are intertwined and interdependent.
there is no single, one-best-way approach to change management.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the global players in the industry are not only global, but also national.
the globalization of the work system is not a one-way process.
the national institutional contexts have a significant impact on the way the MNCs organize their subsidiaries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the national institutional context of MNCs is a crucial factor for understanding the design of work systems in subsidiaries.
global and national effects are intertwined in the design of MNCs.
the global and the national effects on change management processes in MNCs are not contradictory but complementary.
